extracted.intended_audience: researchers working on peer-review/reviewer-assignment algorithms, conference reviewers, and machine-learning researchers interested in evaluation and datasets
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, evaluating, and reporting experiments that measure how well algorithms compute similarity scores (reviewer-paper expertise) and releasing a gold-standard dataset of self-reported expertise. Includes survey design, dataset construction, and comparative algorithm evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity score (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of the “similarity score’’ — a numerical estimate of the expertise of a reviewer in reviewing a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central quantity that automated reviewer-assignment approaches compute and which algorithms should estimate. The paper constructs a dataset of self-reported expertise scores to serve as a gold standard for these similarity scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairwise ranking accuracy (0-1 loss)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rankings used as a measure of accuracy: conditioned on easy/hard triple setting, the loss function is the 0-1 loss on whether the algorithm predicts the relative ranking of a pair of papers correct or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pairwise comparisons between two papers to judge if the algorithm orders them correctly for a reviewer; reported experiments use this 0-1 loss as the primary accuracy metric (Section 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Error rates in easy vs hard cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical error rates for ordering two papers range from 12%-30% in easy cases and 36%-43% in hard cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting algorithm performance, separate results by perceived difficulty (easy vs hard triples) because error rates differ substantially; include these ranges to convey typical performance and motivate further research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm input regime (titles/abstracts vs full text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most specialized algorithms are designed to work with titles and abstracts of papers; some methods (e.g., TF-IDF) can use full texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing algorithms, explicitly state what textual inputs were used (titles/abstracts or full text). Performance conclusions may depend on this input regime; e.g., Specter2 performs best in the titles/abstracts regime while TF-IDF using full text is on par with Specter2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative algorithm performance (specialized vs general models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialized similarity-computation algorithms vs off-the-shelf large language models: off-the-shelf LLMs performed worse than specialized algorithms in the reported experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report comparisons across algorithm families (specialized embedding/metadata methods, classical methods like TF-IDF, and off-the-shelf LLMs) and be explicit about training/fine-tuning or lack thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset composition: self-reported expertise scores
rubrics_metrics.description: The released dataset consists of 477 self-reported expertise scores provided by 58 researchers who evaluated their expertise in reviewing papers they have read previously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how expertise labels were elicited (self-report), sample size, and the provenance of participants; make the dataset available and document collection procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope restriction and claim alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope Limitation to Computer Science: the authors state 'Specifically, we conduct a survey of computer science researchers' and restrict claims to computer science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claims and any suggested generalizations are explicitly limited to the surveyed domain (here, computer science); remove or revise statements that over-generalize to other disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report key limitations (sample size & diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge limitations such as sample size and diversity (particularly large fraction from the US); include a 'Key limitations' heading and reiterate limitations in discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly document major limitations in the introduction and discussion so readers and reviewers can interpret results appropriately; if possible, provide quantitative details about participant demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey interface influence and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey interface design can influence the data and evaluations: 'instructions, scoring levels, and level titles all influence reviewer scores.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about the exact instructions and interface used; include the text shown to participants and examples (e.g., what constitutes 'tricky examples') to allow readers to judge interface effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include survey instructions and examples in paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention more details about survey instructions: authors included the text provided to participants containing an example of what was meant by tricky examples in 'expertise evaluations' part of Section 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the exact wording and examples in the paper or supplement so that others can assess how participants interpreted rating scales and labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of dataset definitions and analytic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Address inconsistencies across sections (e.g., 'low expertise is defined [slightly differently in two sections]') and consider standard thresholds (e.g., 1 standard deviation) for defining expertise categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a consistent definition of categories and dataset versions across the paper; when choices vary, report sensitivity analyses and make results available (e.g., via public response or supplement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and code availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide code repository link for experiments and dataset processing: https://github.com/niharshah/goldstandard-reviewer-paper-match
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Release code and data to enable reproducibility. Link to implementation and data processing scripts; document dependencies and experimental settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish primary claims from out-of-scope operational issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational concerns raised by reviewers (privacy, reviewer's speed of response, distribution of review workloads, scaling, encryption) are beyond the claims of this paper, which focuses on accuracy of algorithms w.r.t. self-reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state what is within scope (e.g., accuracy evaluation) and what is out of scope (operational deployment, privacy, scaling); don't conflate separate system-level requirements with dataset/accuracy claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest attribution of contributions (no false claim of algorithmic novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not claim algorithmic contributions if none: the authors emphasize they 'make no claims of new algorithms' and that their claims 'pertain to the new dataset and evaluating existing algorithms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the paper's abstract, introduction, and title reflect actual contributions (dataset release and evaluation) rather than implying novel algorithmic methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to venue submission requirements (length and review criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission Length: Long submission (more than 12 pages of main content). The authors request the resubmission be evaluated according to TMLR's criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the venue's formatting and length policies and evaluate/resubmit according to the venue's stated review criteria; when resubmitting, document changes since last submission and responses to reviewer comments.
